glossary.definition: A ray is an infinitely thin line showing the path along which light energy travels when wavelength goes to zero.
glossary.example: A narrow laser beam in air travels along a straight ray.

glossary.definition: Geometrical optics is the study of light propagation using rays by neglecting the tiny finite wavelength of light.
glossary.example: Tracing rays through eyeglasses or a camera lens uses geometrical optics.

glossary.definition: Diffraction is the spreading of light at the edges of a very small opening because light has a finite wavelength.
glossary.example: A hole smaller than 0.1 mm blurs the sharp shadow on a screen.

glossary.definition: The refractive index n of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum c to its speed v in that medium.
glossary.example: Glass with n = 1.5 slows light to c / 1.5.

glossary.definition: A homogeneous medium is a material whose refractive index has the same constant value at every point.
glossary.example: Calm air at uniform temperature is a homogeneous medium.

glossary.definition: Optical path length is the geometric distance light travels multiplied by the refractive index of the medium.
glossary.example: Travelling 2 cm in glass of n = 1.5 gives an optical path length of 3 cm.

glossary.definition: A stationary path is a path whose travel time does not change to first order when the path is slightly shifted.
glossary.example: At the bottom of a smooth valley, a tiny step sideways does not change height.

glossary.definition: Fermat's principle states that a light ray between two points follows a path whose optical path length is stationary.
glossary.example: Light bends at water so the total travel time stays stationary.

glossary.definition: Refraction is the bending of a light ray when it crosses the boundary between two media of different refractive indices.
glossary.example: A spoon in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface.

glossary.definition: The paraxial approximation restricts rays to small angles with the optical axis so sin θ and tan θ equal θ in radians.
glossary.example: For an angle of 0.05 rad, sin 0.05 is very close to 0.05.

glossary.definition: The center of curvature C is the center of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface forms a part.
glossary.example: A normal line drawn at any point on a spherical surface passes through C.

glossary.definition: A meridional ray is a ray that stays inside a single flat plane containing the optical axis.
glossary.example: Any ray starting from a point on the optical axis is a meridional ray.

glossary.definition: A thin lens is a lens whose thickness is very small compared to the object distance, image distance, and surface radii.
glossary.example: A thin spectacle lens allows all distances to be measured from its center P.

glossary.definition: A principal focus is an axial point paired with rays parallel to the axis either after or before passing through the lens.
glossary.example: Sunlight parallel to the axis meets at the second principal focus F₂.

glossary.definition: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of the transverse image height y' to the transverse object height y.
glossary.example: If a 1 cm object forms an inverted 2 cm image, the lateral magnification is -2.

cards.title: When light behaves like thin straight pencils
cards.meaning: Geometrical optics is the model of light as thin directional lines called rays when openings are much larger than the wavelength.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Point source P shining through a wide aperture onto screen SS prime"><line x1="115" y1="16" x2="115" y2="58" class="lk" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="115" y1="122" x2="115" y2="164" class="lk" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="215" y1="16" x2="215" y2="164" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="32,90 215,34 215,146" class="s"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="34" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="146" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="215" y2="90" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 62 81 A 32 32 0 0 1 62 99" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="32" cy="90" r="4" class="h"/><text x="20" y="94" font-size="12" class="t">P</text><text x="115" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">A</text><text x="115" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">B</text><text x="162" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Ray (λ→0)</text><text x="228" y="28" font-size="11" class="t">S</text><text x="228" y="160" font-size="11" class="t">S'</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the sharp cone of rays from P through wide opening AB onto screen SS'.
cards.example: Visible light has a tiny wavelength near 0.0005 cm, so ordinary lenses and mirrors are huge compared to it.
cards.bridge: In the mathematical limit where wavelength λ goes to zero, diffraction disappears and light energy follows thin paths called rays.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is geometrical optics?
cards.body: Geometrical optics treats light propagation using thin rays by neglecting the finite wavelength of light when apertures are large.

cards.title: Why denser media count as longer paths
cards.meaning: Optical path length is the vacuum distance that light would travel in the same time it takes to cross a medium.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Physical thickness d in glass compared with longer optical path n times d in vacuum"><rect x="65" y="24" width="80" height="52" rx="6" class="s ok"/><line x1="24" y1="50" x2="185" y2="50" class="lk" stroke-width="2.2"/><line x1="65" y1="130" x2="185" y2="130" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="65" cy="130" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="185" cy="130" r="3.5" class="f"/><line x1="65" y1="84" x2="65" y2="142" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="145" y1="84" x2="145" y2="112" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="105" y="44" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Glass (n = 1.5)</text><text x="105" y="68" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">d = 2 cm</text><text x="125" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">L_op = n d = 3 cm</text><text x="125" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Same travel time τ in vacuum</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the 2 cm glass block (top) with the 3 cm vacuum path (bottom) that takes the exact same time.
cards.example: In glass with refractive index n = 1.5, a physical thickness of 2 cm has an optical path length of 1.5 × 2 cm = 3 cm.
cards.bridge: Because speed in a medium is c / n, the time for step ds is (n ds) / c, so integrating n ds gives the optical path length.

cards.label: 02 · Definition
cards.title: What is optical path length?
cards.body: Optical path length is the integral of refractive index n along the geometric path, equal to c times the travel time.

cards.title: How light chooses its path
cards.meaning: Fermat's principle says light travels along a path whose travel time is stationary compared with slightly different nearby paths.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Actual stationary ray path ACB compared with nearby dashed trial paths"><path d="M 30 138 Q 115 32 230 42" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 130 92 230 42" class="hk" stroke-width="2.8"/><path d="M 30 138 Q 148 148 230 42" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 56 116 A 34 34 0 0 1 64 134" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="30" cy="138" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="230" cy="42" r="4" class="f"/><text x="18" y="148" font-size="12" class="t">A</text><text x="238" y="40" font-size="12" class="t">B</text><text x="112" y="52" font-size="11" class="t">Trial path C'</text><text x="128" y="88" font-size="12" class="t">Actual ray C</text><text x="162" y="138" font-size="11" class="t">δ ∫ n ds = 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the solid amber ray ACB between the two dashed trial paths where small shifts do not change travel time.
cards.example: In uniform air, the straight line between A and B has the shortest optical path. Inside an elliptical mirror, every path from focus S₁ to focus S₂ has the exact same length.
cards.bridge: Therefore the modern statement replaces 'least time' with 'stationary optical path length': δ ∫ n ds = 0, allowing a minimum, maximum, or constant value.

cards.label: 03 · Definition
cards.title: What is Fermat's principle?
cards.body: Fermat's principle states that the actual ray path between two points makes the optical path length stationary with respect to small path variations.

cards.label: 04 · Reflection
cards.title: Law of reflection from Fermat's principle
cards.body: Reflecting A across mirror MN to A' makes AP + PB = A'P + PB. A straight line A'PB minimizes length, so angle i equals angle r in one plane.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Reflection at plane mirror MN using image point A prime"><line x1="20" y1="115" x2="240" y2="115" class="lk" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="60" y1="40" x2="60" y2="165" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="135" y1="35" x2="135" y2="115" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="165" x2="135" y2="115" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="60,40 135,115 215,35" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 118 98 A 24 24 0 0 1 135 91" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 135 91 A 24 24 0 0 1 152 98" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="60" cy="40" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="60" cy="165" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="135" cy="115" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="215" cy="35" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="46" y="42" font-size="12" class="t">A</text><text x="42" y="168" font-size="12" class="t">A'</text><text x="68" y="110" font-size="11" class="t">R</text><text x="135" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">P</text><text x="135" y="28" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">S</text><text x="224" y="38" font-size="12" class="t">B</text><text x="118" y="78" font-size="12" class="t">i</text><text x="152" y="78" font-size="12" class="t">r</text><text x="232" y="132" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" class="t">M → N</text></svg>

phases.why: write L_op using Pythagoras in both triangles

phases.name: Stationary
phases.why: differentiate L_op with respect to x and set to zero

phases.name: Angles
phases.why: replace the triangle ratios with sin θ₁ and sin θ₂

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: equate the two products

steps.note: Write optical path \(n_1 AR + n_2 RB\) from the two right triangles.
Differentiate with respect to \(x\); the second term gets a minus sign.

ask.q: How do we find the stationary ray path as \(x\) varies?
ask.why: Fermat's principle requires the derivative of optical path with respect to \(x\) to vanish.

steps.note: Set the derivative equal to zero for an extremum.

ask.q: What condition must \(dL_{op}/dx\) satisfy on the actual ray?
ask.why: At a stationary point of the optical path, the first derivative is zero.

steps.note: In the triangles, \(\sin\theta_1 = x/AR\) and \(\sin\theta_2 = (L-x)/RB\).

ask.q: What does \(x / \sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) equal in triangle \(AMR\)?
ask.why: Side \(x\) is opposite \(\theta_1\) and \(\sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) is the hypotenuse.

steps.note: Add \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) to both sides.

ask.q: Which move isolates the two refraction terms on opposite sides?
ask.why: Adding \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) places \(n_1\sin\theta_1\) and \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) on opposite sides.

steps.note: Snell's law of refraction.

cards.label: 06 · Example
cards.title: Parabolic and elliptical reflectors
cards.body: A paraboloid reflects parallel rays to its focus (dish antennas). An ellipse reflects every ray from focus \(S_1\) to focus \(S_2\) with equal travel time (ruby laser).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When does geometrical optics accurately describe light propagation?
options: When wavelength is much smaller than apertures
When apertures are smaller than wavelength
Only when refractive index is zero
cards.why: Neglecting wavelength works when openings are much larger than the wavelength of light.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to the modern Fermat's principle, the optical path of a ray is:
cards.why: The ray path makes the optical path length stationary: a minimum, maximum, or constant.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In a homogeneous medium, light rays travel along ______ lines.
cards.why: With constant refractive index, a straight line minimizes the optical path between two points.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find the optical path length for \(4\text{ cm}\) in glass of \(n = 1.5\).
cards.why: Optical path length equals \(n \times d = 1.5 \times 4\text{ cm} = 6\text{ cm}\).

sheets.title: Single spherical surface
sheets.source: Unit 2 · Ghatak §§4.2–4.3 (PDF pp. 80–82). Note: Section 4.1 is missing from the unit files and is not included.

cards.title: Why only rays close to the axis focus sharply
cards.meaning: The paraxial approximation keeps only rays that make very small angles with the symmetry axis of a curved surface.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Paraxial ray making a small angle alpha with the optical axis at height h"><line x1="16" y1="105" x2="244" y2="105" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 132 24 Q 104 105 132 162" class="lk" stroke-width="2.4"/><line x1="118" y1="56" x2="118" y2="105" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="28,105 118,56 226,105" class="hk" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 56 90 A 32 32 0 0 1 60 105" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 196 105 A 30 30 0 0 1 199 93" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="28" cy="105" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="56" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="226" cy="105" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="28" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">O</text><text x="68" y="98" font-size="11" class="t">α</text><text x="126" y="84" font-size="11" class="t">h</text><text x="118" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">P</text><text x="226" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">I</text><text x="130" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Small α: sin α ≈ tan α ≈ h/x</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the small angle arc α near O where height h divided by distance x gives the angle in radians.
cards.example: At an angle of 0.1 rad (about 5.7°), sin(0.1) = 0.0998 and tan(0.1) = 0.1003, so sin φ ≈ tan φ ≈ φ.
cards.bridge: Under this small-angle rule, all paraxial rays from object point O take equal time and meet at a single image point I.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is the paraxial approximation?
cards.body: The paraxial approximation assumes rays make very small angles with the optical axis so sine and tangent equal the angle in radians.

cards.label: 02 · Sign convention
cards.title: Cartesian sign convention at pole P
cards.body: Light enters from the left. With pole P as origin, distances to the right are positive, to the left are negative, and upward heights are positive.

phases.why: express φ₁ and φ₂ using h, x, y, and r

steps.note: For small paraxial angles, \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\) in Snell's law.
Use exterior angles of triangles \(OSC\) and \(ISC\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), what does exterior angle \(\phi_1\) equal?
ask.why: Angle \(\phi_1\) is the exterior angle to interior angles \(\alpha_1\) and \(\beta\).

steps.note: Replace small angles by height \(h\) over horizontal distances.

ask.q: Under the paraxial approximation, how is angle \(\alpha_1\) written?
ask.why: For small angles, \(\alpha_1 \approx \tan\alpha_1 = h / x\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(h\) so ray height cancels out.

ask.q: Why does dividing by \(h\) show all paraxial rays focus together?
options: The equation no longer depends on \(h\)
ask.why: Once \(h\) cancels, every paraxial ray gives the same image distance \(y\).

steps.note: Collect \(x, y\) terms on the left and \(r\) terms on the right.
Apply the Cartesian sign convention with \(O\) on the left (\(u = -x\)).

ask.q: Since object \(O\) lies left of pole \(P\), what replaces \(x\)?
ask.why: Distances to the left of \(P\) are negative, so \(u = -x\) and \(x = -u\).

cards.title: Rays that stay in one flat slice versus skew rays
cards.meaning: Meridional rays stay inside the plane that contains the optical axis, whereas skew rays twist out of a single plane.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Meridional ray staying inside the axial plane versus a skew ray twisting out"><polygon points="24,118 76,34 236,34 184,118" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="76" x2="226" y2="76" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="52,76 128,48 204,76" class="hk" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 76 67 A 26 26 0 0 1 78 76" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><polyline points="64,108 134,58 196,144" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="52" cy="76" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="204" cy="76" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="46" y="92" font-size="11" class="t">C₁</text><text x="208" y="92" font-size="11" class="t">C₂</text><text x="134" y="44" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Meridional ray (in plane)</text><text x="148" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Skew ray (leaves plane)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the amber meridional ray inside the flat axial slice, while the dashed skew ray leaves the slice.
cards.example: Every ray starting from an object point on the optical axis is automatically a meridional ray.
cards.bridge: When a system has two spherical surfaces, the line joining their centers C₁ and C₂ defines the optical axis.

cards.label: 04 · Definition
cards.title: What is a meridional ray?
cards.body: A meridional ray is a light ray confined to a single plane containing the optical axis, unlike a non-planar skew ray.

cards.label: 05 · Derivation
cards.title: Mirror equation for a single spherical surface
cards.legend: Spherical mirror \(SPM\) with object \(O\), center \(C\), image \(I\) all to the left of pole \(P\) (\(u = -x, v = -y, R = -r\)).

phases.name: Reflection law
phases.why: equate angles of incidence and reflection

phases.name: Triangle angles
phases.why: write φ₁ and φ₂ in terms of α₁, α₂, and β

phases.name: Paraxial ratios
phases.why: substitute h/x, h/y, and h/r and cancel h

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: replace x, y, r with -u, -v, -R

steps.note: At point \(S\), the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Use exterior angles of triangles \(OSC\) and \(CSI\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), how is \(\phi_1\) related to \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_1\)?
ask.why: Exterior angle \(\beta\) equals \(\alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\).

steps.note: Replace each small angle by height \(h\) divided by distance.

ask.q: What replaces \(\beta\) in the paraxial approximation?
ask.why: Normal \(CS\) meets the axis at distance \(r\), so \(\beta \approx h / r\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(h\).

ask.q: What is the next step to simplify the height \(h\) out?
ask.why: Every term has \(h\) in the numerator, so dividing by \(h\) removes it.

steps.note: Collect \(1/x + 1/y\) on the left and \(2/r\) on the right.
With \(O, I, C\) on the left of \(P\), minus signs cancel on both sides.

ask.q: Which substitution converts the refraction formula into the mirror formula?
ask.why: Setting \(n_2 = -n_1\) in \(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\) gives \(\frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R}\).

cards.label: 06 · Example
cards.title: Worked example: refraction at a spherical surface
cards.body: An object in air (\(n_1 = 1\)) lies \(40\text{ cm}\) left of a convex glass surface (\(n_2 = 1.5, R = +15\text{ cm}\)). The paraxial image forms at \(+180\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In the Cartesian sign convention, when is object distance \(u\) positive?
options: When incident rays converge right of P
When a real object sits left of P
cards.why: Distances to the right of pole \(P\) are positive, which happens for a virtual object.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Off-axis rays that do not stay in a single plane are called ______ rays.
cards.why: Rays confined to the axial plane are meridional rays; non-planar rays are skew rays.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For a concave mirror with \(R = -60\text{ cm}\) and \(u = -80\text{ cm}\), find \(v\).

cards.title: Two spherical surfaces pressed close together
cards.meaning: A thin lens is a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces whose thickness is negligible compared to all other distances.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Thin lens of tiny thickness t compared with distances u and v measured from center P"><line x1="12" y1="96" x2="248" y2="96" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 118 26 Q 104 96 118 164 Q 132 96 118 26" class="s ok"/><polyline points="26,96 118,46 218,96" class="hk" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 50 83 A 28 28 0 0 1 54 96" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 192 96 A 26 26 0 0 1 195 84" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="26" cy="96" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="118" cy="96" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="218" cy="96" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="26" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">O</text><text x="118" y="20" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">t ≪ |u|, |v|</text><text x="114" y="114" text-anchor="end" font-size="12" class="t">P</text><text x="218" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">I</text><text x="72" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">u (from P)</text><text x="168" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">v (from P)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the thin lens at P: thickness t is so small that both u and v are measured from P.
cards.example: Because thickness t is tiny, we measure object distance u and image distance v from one shared center P.
cards.bridge: The first surface forms an intermediate image Q at v', which immediately acts as the object for the second surface to form final image I at v.

cards.label: 01 · Definition
cards.title: What is a thin spherical lens?
cards.body: A thin spherical lens is a medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces whose thickness is negligible compared to object, image, and curvature distances.

cards.label: 02 · Derivation
cards.title: Thin lens and Lensmaker's formula
cards.legend: Lens of index \(n_2\) in medium \(n_1\) with radii \(R_1, R_2\), intermediate image \(Q\) at \(v'\), and relative index \(n = n_2 / n_1\).
cards.setup: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Successive refractions at the two surfaces of a thin lens"><line x1="12" y1="98" x2="248" y2="98" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 110 28 Q 92 98 110 164" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 118 28 Q 136 98 118 164" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="118" y1="50" x2="238" y2="98" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="24,98 110,50 118,50 188,98" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M 46 86 A 25 25 0 0 1 49 98" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 166 98 A 22 22 0 0 1 169 86" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="24" cy="98" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="114" cy="98" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="188" cy="98" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="238" cy="98" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="24" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">O</text><text x="68" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">u < 0</text><text x="114" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">n₂</text><text x="60" y="36" font-size="12" class="t">n₁</text><text x="175" y="36" font-size="12" class="t">n₁</text><text x="114" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">P</text><text x="152" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">v</text><text x="188" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">I</text><text x="238" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">Q (v')</text><text x="130" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0</text></svg>

phases.name: First surface
phases.why: refraction from n₁ into n₂ forms image Q at v'

phases.name: Add second
phases.why: add the second surface refraction from n₂ into n₁

phases.name: Divide by n₁
phases.why: introduce relative index n = n₂ / n₁

phases.name: Focal length
phases.why: define 1/f as the right-hand side

steps.note: First surface \(R_1\) refracts light from \(n_1\) into \(n_2\), forming \(Q\) at \(v'\).
Add the second surface equation \(\frac{n_1}{v} - \frac{n_2}{v'} = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{R_2}\); \(v'\) cancels.

ask.q: Why do we add the two surface equations together?
ask.why: Adding \(+n_2/v'\) and \(-n_2/v'\) eliminates the intermediate image position \(v'\).

steps.note: Factor \((n_2 - n_1)\) on the right, flipping the sign on \(1/R_2\).

ask.q: When \((n_2 - n_1)\) is factored out of \((n_1 - n_2)/R_2\), what remains?
ask.why: Since \(n_1 - n_2 = -(n_2 - n_1)\), factoring out \((n_2 - n_1)\) leaves \(-1/R_2\).

steps.note: Divide by \(n_1\) and write \(n = n_2 / n_1\).

ask.q: What does \((n_2 - n_1) / n_1\) simplify to when \(n = n_2 / n_1\)?
ask.why: Dividing term by term gives \(n_2/n_1 - n_1/n_1 = n - 1\).

steps.note: Define focal power \(1/f\) to get the thin lens formula.

ask.q: When \(u = -\infty\) (incident parallel rays), what does \(v\) equal?
ask.why: Setting \(1/u = 0\) in \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) gives \(v = f\).

cards.label: 03 · Surrounding medium
cards.title: When a biconvex lens diverges light
cards.body: For a biconvex lens (R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0), 1/R₁ - 1/R₂ is positive. It converges light when n₂ > n₁, but diverges light when placed in a medium with n₁ > n₂.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Biconvex lens converging when n2 is greater than n1 and diverging when n2 is less than n1"><line x1="14" y1="50" x2="120" y2="50" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M 62 18 Q 50 50 62 82 Q 74 50 62 18" class="s ok"/><polyline points="18,32 62,32 108,50" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="18,68 62,68 108,50" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="108" cy="50" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="62" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">n₂ > n₁: converges</text><line x1="140" y1="50" x2="246" y2="50" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M 192 18 Q 180 50 192 82 Q 204 50 192 18" class="s ok"/><polyline points="148,32 192,32 238,16" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><polyline points="148,68 192,68 238,84" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="156" y1="50" x2="192" y2="32" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="156" cy="50" r="4" class="h"/><text x="192" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">n₂ < n₁: diverges</text><text x="130" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">1/f = (n₂/n₁ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂)</text></svg>

cards.title: The two special focal points of any lens
cards.meaning: The first principal focus F₁ turns rays from a point into parallel rays, while the second principal focus F₂ collects incoming parallel rays to a point.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="First principal focus F1 and second principal focus F2 of a converging lens"><line x1="12" y1="90" x2="248" y2="90" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 130 20 Q 116 90 130 160 Q 144 90 130 20" class="s ok"/><polyline points="56,90 130,136 238,136" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="22,44 130,44 204,90" class="hk" stroke-width="2.6"/><path d="M 76 90 A 20 20 0 0 1 73 101" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 184 90 A 20 20 0 0 1 187 79" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="56" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="130" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="90" r="4" class="h"/><text x="56" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">F₁</text><text x="124" y="106" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" class="t">P</text><text x="204" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" class="t">F₂</text><text x="80" y="36" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Ray 2 (parallel → F₂)</text><text x="184" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">Ray 1 (F₁ → parallel)</text><text x="92" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">f₁ < 0</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">f₂ > 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Ray 1 from F₁ emerging parallel, and parallel Ray 2 meeting the axis at F₂.
cards.example: For a converging lens of focal length 20 cm in air, F₁ sits at f₁ = -20 cm (left) and F₂ sits at f₂ = +20 cm (right).
cards.bridge: Setting v = ∞ gives u = f₁ (first focal length), and setting u = -∞ gives v = f₂ (second focal length).

cards.label: 04 · Definition
cards.title: What are the first and second principal foci?
cards.body: The first principal focus F₁ is the axial object point whose refracted rays emerge parallel (v = ∞), and the second principal focus F₂ is the axial image point for incident parallel rays (u = -∞).

cards.label: 05 · Ray tracing
cards.title: Three principal rays for graphical image construction
cards.body: Ray 1 through F₁ exits parallel to the axis. Ray 2 parallel to the axis passes through F₂. Ray 3 through lens center P passes undeviated.

cards.label: 06 · Different media
cards.title: Thin lens with different media on its two sides
cards.body: When medium \(n_1\) is on the left and \(n_3\) on the right, setting \(v = \infty\) and \(u = -\infty\) gives \(f_2 / f_1 = -n_3 / n_1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a converging lens in air, what are the signs of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\)?
cards.why: For a converging lens, \(F_1\) lies on the left (\(f_1 < 0\)) and \(F_2\) lies on the right (\(f_2 > 0\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How does a glass biconvex lens behave inside a liquid of higher refractive index?
cards.why: When \(n_2 < n_1\), \((n - 1)\) becomes negative, so \(f < 0\) and the biconvex lens diverges light.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A paraxial ray passing through the center \(P\) of a thin lens travels ______.
cards.why: At \(u = 0\), the thin lens formula gives \(v = 0\), so the ray through \(P\) passes undeviated.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find \(f\) in air for \(n = 1.5\), \(R_1 = +20\text{ cm}\), and \(R_2 = -20\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: 01 · Focal distances
cards.title: Measuring object and image from the two foci
cards.body: Instead of measuring from lens center P, Newton's method measures object position x₁ from F₁ (x₁ = u - f₁) and image position x₂ from F₂ (x₂ = v - f₂).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Distances x1 and x2 measured from principal foci F1 and F2"><line x1="10" y1="86" x2="250" y2="86" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 125 20 Q 113 86 125 152 Q 137 86 125 20" class="s ok"/><line x1="32" y1="86" x2="32" y2="40" class="lk" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="222" y1="86" x2="222" y2="132" class="lk" stroke-width="2.5"/><polyline points="32,40 125,40 222,132" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><polyline points="32,40 80,86 125,132 222,132" class="hk" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M 64 71 A 22 22 0 0 0 58 86" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M 96 101 A 22 22 0 0 0 102 86" class="lk" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="80" cy="86" r="4" class="h"/><circle cx="170" cy="86" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="32" y="32" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">y</text><text x="32" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">O</text><text x="80" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">F₁</text><text x="120" y="102" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" class="t">P</text><text x="170" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">F₂</text><text x="222" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">I</text><text x="236" y="122" font-size="11" class="t">-y'</text><text x="56" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">-x₁</text><text x="102" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">-f₁</text><text x="148" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">f₂</text><text x="196" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" class="t">x₂</text></svg>

cards.label: 02 · Derivation
cards.title: Newton's lens formula
cards.legend: Object height \(y\) at \(x_1\) from \(F_1\), image height \(y'\) at \(x_2\) from \(F_2\), focal lengths \(f_1, f_2\).

phases.name: First focus
phases.why: use similar triangles AOF₁ and LPF₁

phases.name: Second focus
phases.why: use similar triangles KPF₂ and BIF₂

phases.name: Cross-multiply
phases.why: obtain the general Newtonian formula f₁f₂ = x₁x₂

phases.name: Same medium
phases.why: set f₁ = -f and f₂ = f

steps.note: Similar right triangles \(AOF_1\) and \(LPF_1\) share angle at \(F_1\).
In similar triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\), \(-y'/y = x_2/f_2\).

ask.q: In triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\), what does \(-y' / y\) equal?
ask.why: Since \(KP = y\) and \(BI = -y'\), the ratio of heights equals \(x_2 / f_2\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(x_1 f_2\) to get the Newtonian lens formula.

ask.q: Which move clears both denominators in \(f_1/x_1 = x_2/f_2\)?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(x_1 f_2\) gives \(f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_2\).

steps.note: When both sides have the same medium, \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\).

ask.q: When the same medium surrounds the lens, what is \(f_1 f_2\)?
ask.why: Because \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = +f\), their product is \(-f^2\).

steps.note: Thus \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) always have opposite signs.

ask.q: Since \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2 < 0\), what must be true of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)?
ask.why: A negative product \(-f^2\) means one lies left of its focus and the other lies right.

cards.title: How tall and which way up the image is
cards.meaning: Lateral magnification compares the height of the image to the height of the object, including a sign for orientation.

cards.picture: Look at the equal angle arcs θ at lens center P: similar right triangles give m = y'/y = v/u.
cards.example: A positive magnification (m > 0) means an erect image; a negative magnification (m < 0) means an inverted image.
cards.bridge: For a thin lens in one medium, similar triangles through pole P give m = y' / y = v / u = -f₁ / x₁ = -x₂ / f₂.

cards.label: 03 · Definition
cards.title: What is lateral magnification?
cards.body: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of image height y' to object height y, where positive m means erect and negative m means inverted.

cards.label: 04 · Derivation
cards.title: Lateral magnification of spherical surface and thin lens
cards.legend: Object \(OA = y\) at \(u\), center of curvature \(C\) at \(R\), image \(IB = y'\) at \(v\).

phases.name: Triangles at C
phases.why: use similar triangles AOC and ICB through center C

phases.name: Surface law
phases.why: substitute the Gaussian surface relation

phases.name: Single surface
phases.why: obtain m = n₁v / (n₂u)

phases.name: Thin lens
phases.why: multiply m₁ and m₂ for the two lens surfaces

steps.note: Ray \(ACB\) along the normal at \(C\) passes undeviated, giving similar triangles \(AOC\) and \(ICB\).
From \(\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}\), the ratio \(\frac{v-R}{-u+R}\) equals \(-\frac{n_1 v}{n_2 u}\).

ask.q: Why does the ray from \(A\) through \(C\) pass straight without bending?
options: It hits the spherical surface along the normal
ask.why: Any line through center of curvature \(C\) is normal to the sphere, so \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0\).

steps.note: Negate both sides and write \(m_1 = y'/y\) for the first lens surface (image at \(v'\)).

ask.q: What is the lateral magnification of a single surface from \(n_1\) to \(n_2\)?
ask.why: Refraction into medium \(n_2\) weights the ratio \(v/u\) by \(n_1/n_2\).

steps.tex: m_1 m_2 = \frac{n_1 v'}{n_2 u}\cdot\frac{n_2 v}{n_1 v'}
steps.note: Multiply by the second surface magnification \(m_2 = \frac{n_2 v}{n_1 v'}\).

ask.q: How is total magnification \(m\) found for two surfaces in succession?
ask.why: The first image height is scaled again by \(m_2\), so total magnification is \(m_1 m_2\).

steps.note: Both \(n_1/n_2\) and intermediate distance \(v'\) cancel out.

ask.q: Which factors cancel when \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are multiplied?
ask.why: Factors \(n_1, n_2\) and intermediate image distance \(v'\) cancel, leaving \(m = v/u\).

cards.label: 05 · Example
cards.title: Two thin lenses separated by 8 cm (Example 4.3)
cards.body: Convex lens (\(f_1 = +20\text{ cm}\)) with \(u_1 = -40\text{ cm}\) gives \(v_1 = +40\text{ cm}\). Concave lens (\(f_2 = -10\text{ cm}\)) 8 cm behind has virtual object \(u_2 = +32\text{ cm}\), giving \(v_2 \approx -14.5\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is Newton's lens formula when the same medium is on both sides?
cards.why: With the same medium on both sides, \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\), so \(x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2 = -f^2\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does a negative lateral magnification \(m < 0\) indicate?
cards.why: Since \(m = y'/y\), a negative value means \(y'\) and \(y\) have opposite signs (inverted).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A thin lens in air has \(f = 10\text{ cm}\) and \(x_1 = -20\text{ cm}\). Find \(x_2\).
